title: DAG-guided covariate adjustment
whyItMatters: Adjustment can create bias when variables are chosen from significance or availability rather than a causal model.
coreConcept: Draw the assumed causal graph first; seek a sufficient set that blocks backdoor paths without conditioning on colliders or descendants of exposure.
minimalExample: In a treatment–survival study, severity drives treatment and outcome, while a post-treatment complication lies on the causal pathway.
commonWrongPractice: Adjust for every recorded variable, including the complication, because more covariates always reduce confounding.
reviewerAttack: Which arrows justify each adjustment variable, and did conditioning open a collider path or remove part of the effect?
whenToUse: Use before causal regression, weighting, matching, or standardization to make identification assumptions explicit.
whenNotToUse: Do not treat a DAG as empirical proof of the arrows or as a cure for unmeasured confounding.

title: Estimand before estimator
whyItMatters: A technically correct model can answer the wrong clinical question when population, intervention, outcome, time horizon, or intercurrent events are vague.
coreConcept: Specify the target population, treatment strategies, outcome summary, time origin, follow-up, intercurrent-event handling, and causal contrast before selecting an estimator.
minimalExample: A trial asks whether initiating therapy reduces 2-year mortality regardless of later discontinuation.
commonWrongPractice: Choose Cox regression first and let the available variables define the question afterward.
reviewerAttack: What exact quantity would this analysis estimate if every model assumption held?
whenToUse: Use at protocol, analysis-plan, and reviewer stages for trials, observational effects, and prediction tasks.
whenNotToUse: Do not collapse distinct treatment-policy, while-on-treatment, and hypothetical questions into one hazard ratio.

title: Target-trial emulation protocol
whyItMatters: Observational treatment comparisons are vulnerable to immortal-time and selection biases when eligibility, assignment, and time zero are misaligned.
coreConcept: Write the hypothetical trial protocol—eligibility, strategies, assignment, time zero, follow-up, outcome, contrast, and analysis—then emulate each element with observed data.
minimalExample: Compare statin initiation versus no initiation among eligible clinic attendees, assigning strategy and follow-up at the same visit.
commonWrongPractice: Classify anyone who ever initiates during follow-up as treated from baseline.
reviewerAttack: Were eligibility, treatment classification, and follow-up aligned at a common time zero?
whenToUse: Use for causal questions about interventions when randomized evidence is unavailable and longitudinal observational data are adequate.
whenNotToUse: Do not claim the framework repairs unmeasured confounding, poor measurement, or positivity violations.

title: Immortal-time bias
whyItMatters: Misclassified survival time can guarantee event-free exposure time and manufacture a treatment advantage.
coreConcept: Exposure status and risk time must be defined so participants cannot contribute pre-exposure time to the exposed group; use aligned assignment, landmarks, or time-varying exposure as appropriate.
minimalExample: Transplant recipients must survive from diagnosis until transplant, but all that time is labeled exposed.
commonWrongPractice: Compare ever-transplanted with never-transplanted from diagnosis using a baseline group indicator.
reviewerAttack: Could a participant have the event during the time counted as exposed before actually receiving exposure?
whenToUse: Use when exposure, response, or biomarker status is determined after cohort entry.
whenNotToUse: Do not select a landmark after inspecting outcomes or ignore the changed target population among landmark survivors.

title: Time-varying confounding affected by prior treatment
whyItMatters: Standard time-updated regression can adjust away treatment pathways or induce bias when a confounder is itself changed by earlier treatment.
coreConcept: When longitudinal confounders both predict future treatment/outcome and are affected by prior treatment, identify an appropriate longitudinal causal method such as inverse-probability-weighted marginal structural models.
minimalExample: Disease severity changes after each dose and determines both later dosing and mortality.
commonWrongPractice: Put current severity and current dose into a standard Cox model and interpret the dose coefficient causally.
reviewerAttack: Is any time-updated confounder also downstream of earlier exposure?
whenToUse: Use for sustained treatment strategies with repeated treatment and confounder measurements under adequate positivity and measurement.
whenNotToUse: Do not use unstable weights without diagnostics, truncation rationale, and sensitivity analysis.

title: Competing-risk estimand choice
whyItMatters: Cause-specific hazards and cumulative incidence answer different questions when other event types preclude the event of interest.
coreConcept: Choose the estimand first: cause-specific hazard for instantaneous etiologic rate among event-free individuals, or cumulative incidence/risk for prognosis in the presence of competing events.
minimalExample: Relapse is impossible after non-relapse death during leukemia follow-up.
commonWrongPractice: Censor deaths and interpret one minus Kaplan–Meier as the relapse probability.
reviewerAttack: Does the analysis estimate a transition rate or the real-world probability of the event by time t?
whenToUse: Use whenever mutually exclusive event types alter who remains able to experience the outcome.
whenNotToUse: Do not interpret a subdistribution hazard ratio as a cause-specific hazard or a direct biological effect.

title: Restricted cubic splines
whyItMatters: Forcing a continuous predictor to be linear or splitting it at a data-driven cutpoint can hide or invent clinically important shape.
coreConcept: Model plausible smooth nonlinearity with a prespecified number and placement of knots, inspect the fitted function with uncertainty, and test the contribution of nonlinear terms.
minimalExample: Risk rises slowly across moderate age and sharply after older ages without a true threshold.
commonWrongPractice: Search every age cutpoint and report the smallest log-rank P value.
reviewerAttack: Was the functional form prespecified, and are tails supported by enough observations?
whenToUse: Use when a continuous exposure or predictor may have a smooth nonlinear relation and sample size supports flexible parameters.
whenNotToUse: Do not extrapolate beyond data support or interpret visually noisy tails as thresholds.

title: Missingness mechanism audit
whyItMatters: The observed missing-data pattern does not by itself establish MCAR, MAR, or MNAR, yet those assumptions determine valid analysis.
coreConcept: Describe missingness by variable, group, time, and outcome proxies; use subject-matter knowledge to state the assumed mechanism and sensitivity analyses for departures.
minimalExample: Sicker patients skip quality-of-life visits, with severity partly recorded before dropout.
commonWrongPractice: A nonsignificant Little test proves missing completely at random.
reviewerAttack: What unobserved values could still drive missingness after conditioning on recorded variables?
whenToUse: Use before complete-case analysis, imputation, weighting, or joint modeling.
whenNotToUse: Do not label the mechanism solely from a statistical test on observed data.

title: Substantive-model-compatible imputation
whyItMatters: An imputation model that omits outcomes, interactions, nonlinear terms, clustering, or time structure can be incompatible with the final analysis.
coreConcept: Include variables that predict missingness and values, preserve the analysis model's structure, create multiple datasets, analyze each identically, and combine estimates with Rubin-style rules.
minimalExample: A survival model uses a biomarker spline and treatment interaction, while biomarker values are incomplete.
commonWrongPractice: Mean-impute the biomarker before deriving the spline and report ordinary standard errors.
reviewerAttack: Does the imputation model preserve every nonlinear, interaction, outcome, and multilevel feature used downstream?
whenToUse: Use under a defensible MAR assumption when adequate auxiliary variables and a compatible imputation model are available.
whenNotToUse: Do not present imputation as eliminating MNAR uncertainty; include sensitivity analysis when departures matter.

title: Clustered outcomes and inference
whyItMatters: Repeated, site-level, family-level, or cell-level observations violate independent-error assumptions and can make standard errors too small.
coreConcept: Identify the independent assignment/sampling unit and choose a marginal or conditional model whose correlation structure and degrees of freedom match the design.
minimalExample: Twenty hospitals contribute 4,000 patients, but intervention is assigned by hospital.
commonWrongPractice: Analyze all 4,000 patients independently because the patient is the outcome unit.
reviewerAttack: How many independent units identify the treatment contrast, and are small-cluster corrections needed?
whenToUse: Use for cluster trials, multi-center cohorts, repeated measures, families, images, fields, and nested omics data.
whenNotToUse: Do not assume a random intercept repairs treatment-by-cluster confounding or very few independent clusters.

title: Repeated-measures contrast
whyItMatters: A generic time-by-group P value may not correspond to the clinically intended difference at a time point, average response, or trajectory feature.
coreConcept: Prespecify the repeated-measures estimand and covariance/mean structure, use all relevant times, and report contrasts with uncertainty on an interpretable scale.
minimalExample: Symptoms are measured monthly for six months after randomized treatment.
commonWrongPractice: Run separate t tests at each month and highlight whichever is significant.
reviewerAttack: Is the target a month-6 difference, an average over follow-up, or a trajectory contrast, and how was multiplicity handled?
whenToUse: Use for longitudinal continuous or discrete outcomes with within-person correlation.
whenNotToUse: Do not condition interpretation on significance at a selected visit or assume missing visits are ignorable without justification.

title: Negative-control reasoning
whyItMatters: Residual confounding and measurement artifacts often survive conventional adjustment but can be probed with outcomes or exposures that share bias pathways without the target causal pathway.
coreConcept: Choose a negative control with no plausible target causal effect but similar confounding, selection, and measurement structure; interpret a detected association as a bias warning, not a correction.
minimalExample: A prescribing preference instrument appears related to an outcome occurring before treatment initiation.
commonWrongPractice: Because the negative control is null, all unmeasured confounding is ruled out.
reviewerAttack: Why should the control share the relevant bias mechanism, and what violations could make it falsely reassuring?
whenToUse: Use as a falsification probe alongside design-based causal analysis and sensitivity work.
whenNotToUse: Do not treat a null negative control as proof of exchangeability or a non-null result as quantifying the target bias automatically.

title: Diagnostic spectrum and setting
whyItMatters: Accuracy measured in obvious cases and healthy controls rarely transports to the ambiguous population where the test will be used.
coreConcept: Recruit the intended-use spectrum consecutively or randomly, report clinical setting and prior testing, and evaluate accuracy in relevant subgroups.
minimalExample: A cancer assay is developed on late-stage cases versus young healthy volunteers but intended for symptomatic clinic referrals.
commonWrongPractice: Report the case-control AUC as expected screening performance.
reviewerAttack: Does the evaluation population reproduce disease severity, alternatives, prevalence, and work-up of intended use?
whenToUse: Use for diagnostic and screening test design, appraisal, and external evaluation.
whenNotToUse: Do not transport predictive values across prevalence or spectrum without explicit recalculation and evidence.

title: Reference-standard bias
whyItMatters: An imperfect or differentially applied reference standard can misclassify disease and bias sensitivity or specificity.
coreConcept: Define and blind the reference standard, apply it consistently regardless of index-test result, and account for indeterminate or missing verification.
minimalExample: Only patients with a positive imaging screen receive biopsy; screen-negative patients are assumed disease-free.
commonWrongPractice: Calculate sensitivity among biopsied patients and specificity among everyone else.
reviewerAttack: Who received definitive verification, was it independent of the index test, and how were unresolved cases handled?
whenToUse: Use in diagnostic accuracy studies and clinical label construction for machine learning.
whenNotToUse: Do not call routine-care labels ground truth without auditing how and why they were obtained.

title: Decision threshold and net benefit
whyItMatters: A model can rank well yet cause harm if used at implausible thresholds or with miscalibrated probabilities.
coreConcept: Tie threshold probability to a concrete action and relative false-positive/false-negative harms; compare model, treat-all, and treat-none net benefit over a plausible range.
minimalExample: A recurrence model triggers adjuvant therapy only when predicted risk makes treatment harms acceptable.
commonWrongPractice: Claim clinical utility because the AUC exceeds 0.80.
reviewerAttack: What decision does the threshold encode, are probabilities calibrated, and are comparator strategies realistic?
whenToUse: Use after adequate internal or external evaluation when a prediction is intended to change an action.
whenNotToUse: Do not show decision curves over 0–100% without an intended-use threshold range or uncertainty.

title: Calibration hierarchy
whyItMatters: A single Hosmer–Lemeshow P value or intercept cannot reveal whether risk predictions are systematically too extreme or locally distorted.
coreConcept: Assess calibration-in-the-large, calibration slope, and flexible observed-versus-predicted curves with uncertainty at clinically relevant ranges.
minimalExample: A transported score ranks patients correctly but overpredicts absolute risk twofold.
commonWrongPractice: Declare calibration adequate because a goodness-of-fit test is nonsignificant.
reviewerAttack: Are intercept, slope, and local calibration shown, and is sample size sufficient for the curve?
whenToUse: Use whenever a model outputs probabilities or absolute risks.
whenNotToUse: Do not infer individual-level correctness from group calibration or repair poor transport with unreported refitting.

title: Bootstrap optimism correction
whyItMatters: Apparent performance reuses development data and is optimistic, especially after variable selection and tuning.
coreConcept: Repeat the complete modeling pipeline in bootstrap samples, evaluate each fitted model in bootstrap and original data, and subtract mean optimism from apparent performance.
minimalExample: A 20-parameter survival model is developed in 180 events with backward selection.
commonWrongPractice: Bootstrap only the final fixed formula after selection and call it internally validated.
reviewerAttack: Did every data-driven preprocessing, selection, and tuning step occur inside each resample?
whenToUse: Use for internal validation and shrinkage estimation when the sample should remain available for development.
whenNotToUse: Do not call optimism-corrected performance external validation or use resampling to compensate for a fundamentally inadequate sample.

title: External-evaluation sample size
whyItMatters: Small external cohorts yield unstable calibration, discrimination, and net-benefit estimates even if they contain a traditional minimum number of events.
coreConcept: Plan sample size around precision for calibration-in-the-large, calibration slope, discrimination, and decision-analytic measures across the intended outcome horizon.
minimalExample: A five-year mortality model is evaluated in a new hospital with only 28 deaths.
commonWrongPractice: Call the study adequately powered because it exceeds ten events per predictor in the original model.
reviewerAttack: What precision targets justified participants and events for each performance measure?
whenToUse: Use before collecting or selecting a dataset for independent model evaluation.
whenNotToUse: Do not base external-evaluation size on the number of model coefficients or a universal events threshold.

title: Nested resampling for model selection
whyItMatters: Using the same folds to tune hyperparameters and estimate performance leaks selection information into evaluation.
coreConcept: Place all preprocessing and tuning inside inner resampling and reserve outer folds solely for estimating performance of the full selection procedure.
minimalExample: A transcriptomic classifier selects genes, scales features, tunes regularization, and reports cross-validated AUC.
commonWrongPractice: Select genes once on the full dataset, then cross-validate the classifier.
reviewerAttack: Which data influenced feature selection, scaling, tuning, stopping, and the final reported metric?
whenToUse: Use when performance is estimated while any model or pipeline choice is data-adaptive.
whenNotToUse: Do not average inner-loop scores as an unbiased external performance estimate.

title: Rare-outcome performance
whyItMatters: ROC AUC can look favorable when events are rare while positive predictions remain mostly false.
coreConcept: Report prevalence, calibration, sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and precision–recall behavior at relevant thresholds; connect metrics to intended decisions.
minimalExample: A sepsis alert has 2% event prevalence, AUC 0.88, and 12% positive predictive value at the operational threshold.
commonWrongPractice: Describe the alert as 88% accurate.
reviewerAttack: What happens to false alerts and missed cases at the deployed threshold and prevalence?
whenToUse: Use for rare diagnostic, prognostic, screening, and safety outcomes.
whenNotToUse: Do not compare precision across cohorts without accounting for prevalence or ignore calibration.

title: Prediction-model transportability
whyItMatters: Changes in case mix, measurement, care pathways, outcome incidence, and predictor effects can degrade absolute risk even when ranking persists.
coreConcept: Compare target versus development setting, reproduce the locked pipeline, evaluate calibration and discrimination, and separate original performance from any recalibrated or updated model.
minimalExample: An ICU model trained before a treatment guideline is applied after the guideline changes baseline mortality.
commonWrongPractice: Refit the intercept and predictors in the target cohort, then label the result external validation.
reviewerAttack: Was the original model implemented unchanged, and which transport differences were anticipated?
whenToUse: Use before applying a model across geography, time, device, laboratory, or eligibility setting.
whenNotToUse: Do not hide failed original transport by presenting only an updated model.

title: RNA-seq design matrix
whyItMatters: Differential-expression software cannot recover a biological contrast that is confounded or incorrectly encoded in the design matrix.
coreConcept: Define sample-level experimental units, factors, interactions, blocking, paired structure, and the exact contrast before fitting count models.
minimalExample: Tumor and normal tissues are paired within patients and sequencing batch partly overlaps disease status.
commonWrongPractice: Fit expression by tissue alone and treat each technical library as an independent replicate.
reviewerAttack: Is the contrast estimable separately from patient and batch, and what is the biological replicate?
whenToUse: Use before DESeq2, edgeR, or related bulk/pseudobulk count analyses.
whenNotToUse: Do not add perfectly confounded variables and assume software will choose the causal explanation.

title: Count-model dispersion shrinkage
whyItMatters: Gene-wise variance estimates are unstable with few replicates, and Poisson models understate biological variability.
coreConcept: Negative-binomial workflows estimate mean–dispersion trends and borrow information across genes while preserving gene-specific deviations.
minimalExample: Six RNA-seq samples show variance far above the mean for many genes.
commonWrongPractice: Apply a Poisson test per gene because read counts are integers.
reviewerAttack: How was biological dispersion estimated, moderated, and diagnosed at low counts?
whenToUse: Use for replicated bulk RNA-seq and sample-level pseudobulk counts with compatible library-size normalization.
whenNotToUse: Do not interpret shrinkage as fabricating replicates or use it when the independent sample count is absent.

title: Correlation-aware gene-set testing
whyItMatters: Genes within pathways are correlated, so treating them as independent can make competitive gene-set tests anti-conservative.
coreConcept: Choose competitive versus self-contained hypotheses explicitly and use a method whose null, correlation handling, and sample-level permutation scheme match the design.
minimalExample: A co-regulated interferon module contains dozens of strongly correlated genes.
commonWrongPractice: Run independent hypergeometric tests on every thresholded gene list and rank by nominal P value.
reviewerAttack: What is the gene-set null, how is inter-gene correlation handled, and what unit is permuted?
whenToUse: Use for pathway-level interpretation after a valid sample-level differential analysis.
whenNotToUse: Do not convert enrichment into pathway activation, direction, or causality without supporting measurements.

title: Bulk deconvolution identifiability
whyItMatters: Estimated cell fractions depend on the reference signature, platform, cell-state coverage, and separability of cell types.
coreConcept: Audit signature origin and scale, collinearity, missing cell states, absolute versus relative fractions, and validation against orthogonal measurements or mixtures.
minimalExample: A tumor bulk cohort is deconvolved using immune signatures derived from peripheral blood.
commonWrongPractice: Interpret every estimated fraction as an unbiased cell count in tissue.
reviewerAttack: Could an absent or activated cell state be represented as a mixture of available reference profiles?
whenToUse: Use for hypothesis generation and composition adjustment when reference and mixture assumptions are plausible and evaluated.
whenNotToUse: Do not compare relative fractions as independent outcomes or infer cell-intrinsic expression from bulk mixtures.

title: Proteomics missing-value strategy
whyItMatters: Label-free proteomics mixes stochastic missingness with abundance-dependent censoring, so a universal imputation method can distort groups and variances.
coreConcept: Inspect missingness by intensity, peptide, protein, batch, and group; align imputation or censored modeling with plausible mechanisms and propagate analysis uncertainty.
minimalExample: Low-abundance peptides disappear more often in one acquisition batch, while isolated software failures are scattered.
commonWrongPractice: Replace every missing intensity with a small constant before normalization.
reviewerAttack: Which missing values are plausibly censored versus random, and how does the strategy alter group differences?
whenToUse: Use in label-free proteomics after QC and before differential modeling, with mechanism-specific sensitivity analyses.
whenNotToUse: Do not make condition-specific absence equal biological on/off expression without detection-limit evidence.

title: Doublet detection audit
whyItMatters: Multiplets can create hybrid expression profiles, false transitional states, and misleading rare populations.
coreConcept: Estimate expected doublet rates per capture, use sample-aware detection, inspect QC and marker combinations, and report sensitivity limits for homotypic doublets.
minimalExample: A cluster co-expresses mutually exclusive T-cell and epithelial markers and has high UMI counts.
commonWrongPractice: Label it a novel transdifferentiating population because it lies between clusters in UMAP.
reviewerAttack: Were doublets evaluated before biological naming, and could homotypic doublets remain?
whenToUse: Use during droplet single-cell QC before clustering and state annotation.
whenNotToUse: Do not delete every unusual hybrid state solely from one algorithmic score.

title: Ambient RNA contamination
whyItMatters: Cell-free transcripts can appear broadly across droplets and mimic low-level marker expression in unrelated cell types.
coreConcept: Use empty-droplet/background profiles and cluster-specific markers to estimate contamination, compare corrected and uncorrected results, and retain uncertainty.
minimalExample: Hemoglobin transcripts appear in nearly every cell type from a blood-rich tissue.
commonWrongPractice: Annotate all hemoglobin-positive droplets as erythroid-like cells.
reviewerAttack: Does expression exceed the ambient background expected from lysed abundant cells?
whenToUse: Use for droplet single-cell datasets, especially necrotic, blood-rich, or high-RNA tissues.
whenNotToUse: Do not overcorrect true low-level expression or treat a corrected matrix as ground truth.

title: Single-cell variance stabilization
whyItMatters: Sequencing depth and mean–variance dependence can dominate feature selection and embeddings if normalization assumptions are ignored.
coreConcept: Use a count-aware normalization model, inspect residual depth effects, preserve raw counts for compatible downstream tests, and avoid mixing assay scales silently.

whenNotToUse: Do not assume one normalization is optimal for clustering, visualization, differential testing, and absolute expression simultaneously.

title: Batch integration: remove less, prove more
whyItMatters: Visual batch mixing can be achieved by erasing true biological variation, especially when condition and batch are partially confounded.
coreConcept: Benchmark integration on batch removal and biological conservation, keep unintegrated references, test multiple resolutions, and avoid corrected values for unsupported differential inference.

whenToUse: Use when batches share enough biological states to anchor integration and downstream purpose is explicit.
whenNotToUse: Do not integrate a perfectly confounded design and claim recovery of condition effects.

title: Cell-type annotation evidence
whyItMatters: Single markers, transferred labels, and cluster names can conceal ambiguity, state effects, and reference mismatch.

title: Multi-omics latent-factor interpretation
whyItMatters: Latent factors summarize covariance but can represent technical variation, composition, or scale differences rather than a biological program.
coreConcept: Inspect variance explained by view, feature loadings, sample covariates, robustness, and held-out reconstruction; label factors descriptively before mechanistic interpretation.

reviewerAttack: Does the factor survive batch adjustment and resampling, and which modalities actually contribute?
whenToUse: Use for unsupervised discovery of shared and view-specific variation in aligned multi-omics samples.
whenNotToUse: Do not infer direction, mediation, or causality from a latent covariance factor.
transferPrompt: Apply “Multi-omics latent-factor interpretation” to one current decision: what would you change, verify, or narrow?

title: Supervised multi-omics without leakage
whyItMatters: Outcome-guided feature selection across many modalities can overfit severely if preprocessing or component selection sees evaluation outcomes.
coreConcept: Nest normalization, filtering, component tuning, and feature selection inside resampling; keep patient groups together and reserve a locked external evaluation when possible.
minimalExample: RNA, methylation, and proteomics from 90 patients are integrated to classify response.
commonWrongPractice: Select cross-omic features using all outcome labels, then report cross-validated accuracy on those features.
reviewerAttack: Did any target label influence a feature, component, or tuning choice before its outer-fold prediction?
whenToUse: Use for supervised cross-omics signatures with adequate independent samples and a fully reproducible pipeline.
whenNotToUse: Do not let thousands of molecular measurements substitute for independent patients.
transferPrompt: Apply “Supervised multi-omics without leakage” to one current decision: what would you change, verify, or narrow?

title: Radiomics feature reproducibility
whyItMatters: Scanner, reconstruction, resampling, segmentation, and software definitions can shift radiomics features more than biology.
coreConcept: Standardize feature definitions and image preprocessing, assess segmentation and acquisition robustness, lock the pipeline, and evaluate across scanners and sites.
minimalExample: A texture signature is trained on one reconstruction kernel and tested on a different vendor without harmonization analysis.
commonWrongPractice: Assume features with the same names are identical across packages.
reviewerAttack: Were feature values benchmarked to a standard and robustness tested across plausible acquisition and segmentation variation?
whenToUse: Use before developing or transporting imaging biomarkers.
whenNotToUse: Do not use post-outcome harmonization or filter unstable features on the evaluation cohort.
transferPrompt: Apply “Radiomics feature reproducibility” to one current decision: what would you change, verify, or narrow?

title: Prediction-model development sample size
whyItMatters: A fixed events-per-variable rule ignores outcome prevalence, anticipated model fit, parameter complexity, and desired shrinkage.
coreConcept: Plan participants and events using candidate parameter count, outcome frequency, anticipated performance, global shrinkage, and precision of baseline risk.
minimalExample: A binary model considers 30 parameters with 12% outcome prevalence in 400 participants.
commonWrongPractice: Declare ten events per variable sufficient after counting a categorical predictor as one variable.
reviewerAttack: How many parameters—not labels—are estimated, and what shrinkage and precision criteria are targeted?
whenToUse: Use before collecting data or finalizing candidate predictors for clinical prediction development.
whenNotToUse: Do not reduce parameters post hoc by univariable screening and claim the original sample was adequate.
transferPrompt: Apply “Prediction-model development sample size” to one current decision: what would you change, verify, or narrow?

title: Reporting guideline versus risk of bias
whyItMatters: Complete reporting enables appraisal but does not make a confounded, underpowered, or misclassified study valid.
coreConcept: Use reporting checklists to locate required information, then assess design-specific bias, applicability, precision, and identification separately.
minimalExample: An observational paper reports every STROBE item but exposure is severely misclassified.
commonWrongPractice: Convert checklist completion into a numerical quality score and rank studies by it.
reviewerAttack: Which reported design choices threaten validity even though they are transparently described?
whenToUse: Use during protocol writing, manuscript preparation, evidence extraction, and peer review.
whenNotToUse: Do not treat reporting adherence as proof of methodological quality or causal validity.
transferPrompt: Apply “Reporting guideline versus risk of bias” to one current decision: what would you change, verify, or narrow?

title: Statistical unit
whyItMatters: Inference fails when the unit represented by the sample size is not the independent unit that received exposure or generated the outcome.
coreConcept: The statistical unit is the smallest independent unit about which uncertainty is estimated; measurement units nested within it are not extra replicates.
minimalExample: Six patients each contribute 2,000 cells. For a patient-level disease contrast, n is 6 patients—not 12,000 cells.
commonWrongPractice: Report the number of images, cells, fields, or technical repeats as n while treatment or phenotype varies only between subjects.
reviewerAttack: State the experimental unit, nesting structure, and model used to account for within-subject correlation.
whenToUse: Before choosing any test; explicitly map exposure, outcome, and clustering levels.
whenNotToUse: Do not force all questions to the patient level when a genuinely within-cell estimand is intended; still model dependence.
transferPrompt: For one current analysis, write the exposure unit, measurement unit, and inference unit.

title: Biological replicate
whyItMatters: Biological replication supports generalization across independent biological units; technical replication mainly estimates measurement noise.
coreConcept: A biological replicate is an independently sampled organism, patient, culture, or experimental unit under the design—not another aliquot from the same unit.
minimalExample: Three independently treated organoid lines are biological replicates; three wells seeded from one line are usually technical or nested replicates.
commonWrongPractice: Average technical repeats but still describe every well or sequencing lane as an independent biological n.
reviewerAttack: Were samples independently generated and randomized, or are repeated measurements being counted as replication?
whenToUse: Experimental design, power planning, and any claim intended to generalize beyond the measured material.
whenNotToUse: Technical repeats remain useful for assay precision, but cannot replace biological replication.
transferPrompt: Classify each replicate in your project as biological, technical, or repeated measurement.

title: Pseudoreplication
whyItMatters: Treating correlated observations as independent makes standard errors too small and creates false confidence.
coreConcept: Pseudoreplication occurs when the analysis has more nominal observations than independent experimental units.
minimalExample: Two mice per arm with 20 tissue fields per mouse does not create n=40 independent mice per arm.
commonWrongPractice: Apply a two-sample test to all fields/cells without aggregation, random effects, cluster-robust inference, or another design-aware method.
reviewerAttack: Reanalyze at the independent unit or justify a hierarchical model and report the number of independent units.
whenToUse: Audit nested imaging, organoid, repeated-measures, and single-cell analyses.
whenNotToUse: Large within-unit samples may improve unit-level measurement precision, but not between-unit degrees of freedom.
transferPrompt: Locate one place where your data table has more rows than independent units and document the dependency.

title: Confounding
whyItMatters: An observed exposure–outcome association may reflect a common cause rather than the exposure itself.
coreConcept: A confounder causally affects exposure and outcome and is not a consequence of exposure; adjustment should follow a causal/design rationale, not only P values.
minimalExample: Treatment is preferentially given to fitter patients; survival differences may reflect performance status.
commonWrongPractice: Select covariates solely because they are significant in univariable models or adjust for mediators/colliders.
reviewerAttack: Justify the adjustment set, measurement timing, residual confounding, and whether key confounders were unavailable.
whenToUse: Observational causal questions and comparative effectiveness analyses.
whenNotToUse: Prediction models optimize prediction rather than estimate a causal treatment effect; their covariate logic differs.
transferPrompt: Name one plausible common cause of your main exposure and outcome, and how it is measured.

title: Selection bias
whyItMatters: Conditioning inclusion on factors related to exposure and outcome can distort associations before modeling begins.
coreConcept: Selection bias arises when analyzed participants differ systematically because selection is related to the target relation or outcome observation.
minimalExample: A biomarker study includes only patients with high-quality archived tissue, which is associated with center, era, and survival.
commonWrongPractice: Describe exclusions but assume multivariable adjustment automatically repairs selection.
reviewerAttack: Provide the flow of eligible/included participants, compare exclusions, and define the target population.
whenToUse: Cohort assembly, complete-case samples, tissue availability, case-control sampling, and loss to follow-up.
whenNotToUse: Do not label every lack of representativeness as bias; distinguish internal validity from transportability.
transferPrompt: Draw the eligibility funnel for your cohort and identify where outcome-related selection could enter.

title: Missing data
whyItMatters: Complete-case analysis can lose power and introduce bias when missingness depends on observed or unobserved values.
coreConcept: Missing-data handling depends on the missingness mechanism, analysis model, auxiliary information, and sensitivity to departures from assumptions.
minimalExample: Performance status is more often missing in severely ill patients; dropping them changes the analyzed risk distribution.
commonWrongPractice: Use mean imputation or delete incomplete rows without quantifying missingness by variable and group.
reviewerAttack: Report amount/pattern, justify assumptions, include outcome and predictors in imputation, and compare sensitivity analyses.
whenToUse: Any analysis with incomplete covariates, outcomes, follow-up, or assay measurements.
whenNotToUse: Multiple imputation cannot recover variables never measured or rescue grossly nonidentifiable missing-not-at-random processes without assumptions.
transferPrompt: Create a missingness table and state the most defensible mechanism for the key incomplete variable.

title: Multiple testing
whyItMatters: Testing many hypotheses increases the chance of discoveries produced by noise.
coreConcept: Control an error criterion matched to the claim family—often false discovery rate in discovery omics—and report effect sizes alongside adjusted P values.
minimalExample: At alpha .05, 20,000 null gene tests yield roughly 1,000 nominal positives in expectation.
commonWrongPractice: Use raw P<.05 after genome-wide testing or correct each selectively reported subset separately.
reviewerAttack: Define the hypothesis family, correction method, pre-specification, and handling of exploratory analyses.
whenToUse: Multiple endpoints, subgroup scans, omics features, pathways, and candidate model comparisons.
whenNotToUse: Do not mechanically adjust unrelated, pre-specified single questions into an artificial family without explaining the estimand.
transferPrompt: List the full family of hypotheses behind one reported P value in your project.

title: Effect size vs P value
whyItMatters: Statistical compatibility with a null value is not the magnitude, precision, or importance of an effect.
coreConcept: Interpret the estimate and its uncertainty first; P values are sensitive to sample size and do not measure clinical relevance.
minimalExample: A hazard ratio 1.03 with P<.001 may be precisely trivial; HR 1.8 with a wide CI may be important but uncertain.
commonWrongPractice: Call effects large because P is small, or call groups identical because P>.05.
reviewerAttack: Report absolute and relative effect sizes, confidence intervals, and a clinically meaningful threshold.
whenToUse: Every inferential result.
whenNotToUse: Do not treat a confidence interval as a dichotomous significance test in disguise.
transferPrompt: Rewrite one result sentence beginning with the effect estimate rather than the P value.

title: Confidence interval interpretation
whyItMatters: Intervals communicate effect uncertainty and compatibility better than a significance label.
coreConcept: A frequentist 95% interval is generated by a procedure that covers the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples under model assumptions.
minimalExample: HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.48–1.08 is compatible with meaningful benefit and slight harm; it is not proof of no effect.
commonWrongPractice: Say there is a 95% probability the fixed true parameter lies in this computed interval.
reviewerAttack: Discuss precision, clinically relevant values within the interval, and model/measurement assumptions.
whenToUse: Effect estimates, performance metrics, calibration, subgroup interactions, and absolute risk.
whenNotToUse: Intervals do not capture unmodeled bias, confounding, or data errors.
transferPrompt: Identify the most decision-relevant values still compatible with one interval in your work.

title: Cox proportional hazards
whyItMatters: Cox regression handles censoring but its hazard ratio depends on proportional hazards and correct time/variable specification.
coreConcept: The model compares instantaneous hazards conditional on survival to time t, assuming a covariate effect that is proportional over time unless modeled otherwise.
minimalExample: HR 0.70 compares hazards at a given time among those still at risk; it is not a 30% longer survival time.
commonWrongPractice: Interpret HR as a risk ratio, ignore non-proportionality, dichotomize continuous predictors, or use post-baseline variables as fixed covariates.
reviewerAttack: Check proportional hazards, functional form, censoring, events-per-parameter, and time origin.
whenToUse: Time-to-event outcomes with censoring and a defensible hazard-based estimand.
whenNotToUse: Consider alternative estimands/models when hazards cross, competing events dominate, or absolute risk is the decision target.
transferPrompt: State time zero, event, censoring rule, and the meaning of the HR in your analysis.

title: Multivariable adjustment
whyItMatters: Adjustment can address measured confounding or improve prediction, but unstable or data-driven specifications create biased estimates.
coreConcept: Choose variables based on estimand, causal role, measurement timing, and available information; do not confuse adjusted association with causation.
minimalExample: A prognostic biomarker may be adjusted for stage to test incremental prognosis, while a treatment effect needs a confounding set.
commonWrongPractice: Enter only variables with univariable P<.05, overfit sparse events, or adjust for post-exposure mediators.
reviewerAttack: Explain variable selection, coding, nonlinearity, collinearity, missing data, and parameter-to-information ratio.
whenToUse: Confounding control, prognostic modeling, and precision improvement when prespecified.
whenNotToUse: Adjustment cannot correct unmeasured confounding or biased cohort selection by itself.
transferPrompt: For each adjusted variable, label its role: confounder, precision variable, predictor, mediator, or collider risk.

title: Overfitting
whyItMatters: A model can learn idiosyncrasies of development data and appear more accurate than it will be in new patients.
coreConcept: Overfitting grows when effective model complexity is high relative to information; optimism must be estimated and shrinkage/penalization considered.
minimalExample: Selecting 20 genes and coefficients in 40 events can produce an impressive training C-index but unstable external predictions.
commonWrongPractice: Report apparent performance from the same data used for feature selection and fitting.
reviewerAttack: Quantify effective parameters, internal validation, optimism correction, shrinkage, and external performance.
whenToUse: Audit every model-development workflow, including unsupervised choices followed by outcome comparisons.
whenNotToUse: A simple model is not automatically safe; small samples and data-driven cutpoints still overfit.
transferPrompt: List every data-driven choice made before your final performance estimate.

title: Internal validation
whyItMatters: Internal validation estimates optimism from the full model-development process in the development population.
coreConcept: Bootstrap or repeated cross-validation must repeat preprocessing and feature/model selection inside each resample.
minimalExample: Bootstrap the entire selection-and-fit pipeline, evaluate in out-of-bootstrap data, and estimate optimism in calibration and discrimination.
commonWrongPractice: Use one random train/test split in a small dataset or cross-validate only the final frozen model after global feature selection.
reviewerAttack: Was every adaptive step nested, were enough resamples used, and were calibration and optimism reported?
whenToUse: Model development before transport to a new setting.
whenNotToUse: Internal validation does not establish geographic, temporal, or clinical transportability.
transferPrompt: Draw the boundary of one resampling loop and place every preprocessing step inside or outside it.

title: External validation
whyItMatters: Performance in a meaningfully different population tests transportability and reveals calibration drift.
coreConcept: External validation applies a locked model—including coefficients and preprocessing—to data separate in time, place, or setting, without refitting before evaluation.
minimalExample: A model developed at center A is applied unchanged to later patients from centers B–D, reporting calibration and discrimination.
commonWrongPractice: Call a random holdout from the same source 'external' or tune the model on the validation cohort before reporting performance.
reviewerAttack: How independent and clinically different is the validation sample, and was the original model fully specified and locked?
whenToUse: Before claiming general clinical applicability.
whenNotToUse: Recalibration is useful deployment work but should be reported separately from untouched validation performance.
transferPrompt: Name the dimension—time, geography, center, spectrum—along which your planned validation is genuinely external.

title: C-index
whyItMatters: Discrimination ranks patients but does not show accurate probabilities or clinical usefulness.
coreConcept: The concordance index estimates how often predicted order agrees with observed outcome order among comparable pairs, with censoring-specific estimators for survival data.
minimalExample: C=0.70 means about 70% concordance among evaluable pairs—not that predictions are 70% accurate.
commonWrongPractice: Use C-index alone, compare tiny differences without uncertainty, or calculate it ignoring censoring.
reviewerAttack: Report confidence intervals, calibration, appropriate censoring handling, and incremental value relative to a baseline model.
whenToUse: Ranking performance for prognostic/time-to-event models.
whenNotToUse: Do not infer calibrated absolute risk or clinical net benefit from discrimination alone.
transferPrompt: Identify which decision in your project needs ranking, absolute risk, or both.

title: Calibration
whyItMatters: A model can rank patients well while systematically over- or underestimating their risk.
coreConcept: Calibration compares predicted and observed risk; inspect calibration-in-the-large, slope, and flexible plots rather than a single goodness-of-fit test.
minimalExample: A calibration slope of 0.65 suggests predictions are too extreme in the validation cohort.
commonWrongPractice: Claim calibration from a non-significant Hosmer–Lemeshow test or plot grouped points without uncertainty.
reviewerAttack: Show calibration intercept/slope and a smooth plot at clinically relevant horizons, accounting for censoring.
whenToUse: Any probabilistic prediction model and any external validation.
whenNotToUse: Do not interpret recalibrated performance as untouched transportability.
transferPrompt: Choose the clinically meaningful time horizon and specify how observed risk will be estimated there.

title: Decision curve analysis
whyItMatters: Statistical performance does not establish whether acting on predictions improves decisions.
coreConcept: Decision curves compare net benefit across threshold probabilities against treat-all and treat-none strategies, under explicit relative harm assumptions.
minimalExample: At a 10% treatment threshold, a model may identify more true cases without too many weighted false positives.
commonWrongPractice: Select a favorable threshold after inspection, ignore implausible threshold ranges, or call net benefit proof of real-world benefit.
reviewerAttack: Justify the threshold range, comparator strategies, outcome horizon, and whether predictions were validly estimated.
whenToUse: When a prediction would trigger a clinical action with articulable tradeoffs.
whenNotToUse: Avoid when no decision, threshold, or consequence is defined.
transferPrompt: Write the action triggered by your model and the plausible threshold range for that action.

title: Interaction vs subgroup
whyItMatters: A significant result in one subgroup and a non-significant result in another does not prove the effects differ.
coreConcept: Effect modification is assessed by an interaction contrast on a specified scale, with multiplicity and limited power acknowledged.
minimalExample: Treatment HR is 0.75 in men and 0.95 in women; the interaction test—not separate P values—addresses heterogeneity.
commonWrongPractice: Claim subgroup specificity because only one subgroup crosses P<.05.
reviewerAttack: Was the interaction prespecified, powered, tested directly, and corrected/interpreted for multiplicity?
whenToUse: Questions about differential effects across patient or biological contexts.
whenNotToUse: Do not perform indiscriminate subgroup fishing in sparse data.
transferPrompt: Rewrite one subgroup claim as an explicit interaction hypothesis and name its scale.

title: Competing risks
whyItMatters: A competing event prevents the event of interest; censoring it as if ordinary can misestimate absolute incidence.
coreConcept: Use cumulative incidence for absolute risk; cause-specific and subdistribution hazards answer different etiologic and prediction questions.
minimalExample: Death before recurrence prevents later recurrence and changes the probability of recurrence over time.
commonWrongPractice: Use 1−Kaplan–Meier for cause-specific incidence while censoring competing deaths.
reviewerAttack: Define competing events and align the estimator—cumulative incidence, cause-specific hazard, or subdistribution hazard—with the estimand.
whenToUse: Oncology recurrence, cause-specific mortality, transplant outcomes, and geriatric cohorts.
whenNotToUse: A competing event must preclude the outcome, not merely occur alongside it.
transferPrompt: List events that prevent your primary event and choose whether your target is cause-specific association or absolute risk.

title: Time-dependent bias
whyItMatters: Using future exposure information at baseline can create immortal time or reverse temporal ordering.
coreConcept: Exposure classification and follow-up must respect when information becomes available; model time-varying exposures when appropriate.
minimalExample: Patients classified as 'received maintenance' must survive long enough to receive it; counting earlier survival as exposed biases benefit upward.
commonWrongPractice: Define groups using post-baseline treatment and analyze them as baseline groups.
reviewerAttack: Draw the timeline, define time zero, exposure assignment, grace period, and risk-set membership.
whenToUse: Treatment initiation, response-defined cohorts, dynamic biomarkers, and landmark analyses.
whenNotToUse: Landmark analysis changes the target population; it is not a universal repair.
transferPrompt: Draw time zero and the earliest time each exposure in your study can be known.

title: scRNA cell-level DEG vs pseudobulk
whyItMatters: Cells from the same patient share biology and processing; treating them as independent often inflates false discoveries.
coreConcept: For patient-level conditions, aggregate counts within patient×cell type or use a suitable hierarchical model so biological subjects drive inference.
minimalExample: Compare subtype A vs B using one pseudobulk profile per patient and cell type, with library-size-aware count modeling.
commonWrongPractice: Pool all cells, run Wilcoxon, and report tiny P values without patient-level replication or effect consistency.
reviewerAttack: Show patient numbers, per-patient effects, balance, covariate control, and FDR at the tested feature family.
whenToUse: Patient-level disease, treatment, genotype, or outcome contrasts in single-cell data.
whenNotToUse: Pseudobulk cannot create replication when only one patient exists per group.
transferPrompt: Write the aggregation key and design formula for one planned cell-type DEG analysis.

title: Batch effect
whyItMatters: Technical variation can align with biology and generate or erase apparent signal.
coreConcept: Prevent confounding by design, diagnose with metadata and controls, and correct only under assumptions that preserve relevant biology.
minimalExample: All cases sequenced on run 1 and controls on run 2 make disease inseparable from run.
commonWrongPractice: Apply integration blindly and claim batch is removed because a UMAP mixes.
reviewerAttack: Show the design matrix, batch–condition balance, QC, sensitivity before/after correction, and retained biological signals.
whenToUse: High-throughput studies spanning runs, centers, chemistry versions, plates, or acquisition dates.
whenNotToUse: No algorithm can identify a disease effect perfectly confounded with batch without extra information.
transferPrompt: Cross-tabulate your primary biological group against each technical batch variable.

title: Patient-level replication
whyItMatters: Large numbers of molecular measurements do not substitute for independently sampled patients.
coreConcept: Generalization to patients depends on the number, diversity, and balance of patients, with measurements nested within them.
minimalExample: Five tumors with 50,000 cells each provide five patient-level replicates for a tumor-level exposure.
commonWrongPractice: Advertise cell count as sample size while omitting per-group patient counts and between-patient heterogeneity.
reviewerAttack: Report patient-level distributions and demonstrate the result is not driven by one high-cell-yield sample.
whenToUse: Single-cell, spatial spots, proteomic features, and repeated biopsies.
whenNotToUse: Within-patient mechanistic observations can be valuable but require narrower claims.
transferPrompt: Plot or tabulate the target effect separately for each patient.

title: Cluster annotation
whyItMatters: Annotation errors propagate into abundance, differential expression, communication, and biological narratives.
coreConcept: Annotation integrates multiple positive/negative markers, reference information, tissue context, QC, and uncertainty; labels should match resolution supported by evidence.
minimalExample: A T-cell cluster is supported by CD3 genes, lacks myeloid markers, and is checked against a reference before subtype naming.
commonWrongPractice: Name a cluster from one marker, circularly use the same gene as outcome, or force every cluster to a precise subtype.
reviewerAttack: Provide marker panels, reference mapping, ambiguity, doublet checks, and patient distribution.
whenToUse: Every cell-state analysis before downstream comparisons.
whenNotToUse: Do not treat automated reference labels as ground truth in a diseased or novel tissue.
transferPrompt: For one label, list three positive markers, two exclusion markers, and one plausible alternative.

title: Marker circularity
whyItMatters: Defining a group by a feature and then testing that feature between groups produces a tautological result.
coreConcept: Separate features used to construct labels or select cells from features used to validate or infer biology.
minimalExample: Calling cells CXCL13-high and then presenting higher CXCL13 expression as validation adds no independent evidence.
commonWrongPractice: Use discovery markers to name clusters, score the same program, and claim independent confirmation.
reviewerAttack: Which data/features defined the state, and what orthogonal evidence validates it?
whenToUse: Cluster naming, signature construction, responder definitions, and biomarker cutpoints.
whenNotToUse: Descriptive restatement is acceptable if explicitly labeled, not presented as validation.
transferPrompt: Separate your defining features from your validation features in two lists.

title: Double dipping
whyItMatters: Reusing the same data to select a promising pattern and test it produces optimistic P values and performance.
coreConcept: Selection uncertainty must be included by nested resampling, selective inference, or independent confirmation.
minimalExample: Choose the cutpoint with the smallest survival P value and report that same P value as if the cutpoint were prespecified.
commonWrongPractice: Cluster, select the most separated outcome groups, then run a conventional test ignoring the selection.
reviewerAttack: Enumerate adaptive choices and repeat them inside validation or verify the frozen choice independently.
whenToUse: Feature selection, cutpoint discovery, cluster choice, pathway prioritization, and figure-driven hypotheses.
whenNotToUse: Exploratory reuse is legitimate for hypothesis generation if uncertainty and need for validation are explicit.
transferPrompt: Mark which results in your project are discovery and which used untouched data for confirmation.

title: Pathway enrichment
whyItMatters: Pathway results compress gene-level signals but depend on the gene universe, database, redundancy, and selection procedure.
coreConcept: Interpret enrichment as coordinated annotation-level evidence, not direct pathway activity or mechanism; report method, universe, version, effect direction, and FDR.
minimalExample: An interferon gene set enriched among upregulated genes supports an expression program compatible with interferon response.
commonWrongPractice: Use all genome genes instead of measured/tested genes as background or claim a pathway is activated from an unstratified hit list.
reviewerAttack: Define the universe, gene-set database/version, ranking/statistic, redundancy handling, and leading-edge genes.
whenToUse: Biological interpretation after a valid gene-level analysis.
whenNotToUse: Do not use enrichment to rescue an invalid differential analysis.
transferPrompt: State the tested gene universe and database version for your next enrichment analysis.

title: GSEA vs ORA
whyItMatters: Over-representation and ranked-list enrichment answer different questions and have different selection biases.
coreConcept: ORA tests whether a selected hit list contains excess set members; GSEA-like methods test whether set members concentrate toward extremes of a ranked list.
minimalExample: ORA uses DE genes passing thresholds; GSEA uses the signed statistic for all eligible genes.
commonWrongPractice: Call any pathway tool 'GSEA', ignore ranking direction, or compare results produced from different universes.
reviewerAttack: Why was this method selected, how was the list/rank constructed, and were sample-label rather than gene-label permutations appropriate?
whenToUse: GSEA for distributed coordinated effects; ORA for a well-justified discrete list.
whenNotToUse: Neither method establishes causality or cell-type origin by itself.
transferPrompt: Choose ORA or ranked enrichment for one contrast and justify the input representation.

title: Cell proportion testing
whyItMatters: Cell counts are compositional, overdispersed, and nested within samples; naïve cell-level tests misstate uncertainty.
coreConcept: Compare sample-level proportions or counts with a model respecting replication, composition, depth, covariates, and zero inflation as appropriate.
minimalExample: Estimate one macrophage proportion per patient and model the group effect with patient-level uncertainty.
commonWrongPractice: Pool cells by group and use a chi-square test as if every captured cell were independently sampled.
reviewerAttack: Show per-patient distributions, capture/QC balance, compositional sensitivity, and prespecified cell classes.
whenToUse: Questions about abundance of annotated cell populations across biological units.
whenNotToUse: Captured proportion is not automatically tissue abundance; dissociation and sampling processes matter.
transferPrompt: Plot the target population proportion for every patient and annotate total cells/QC.

title: Differential abundance
whyItMatters: Changes may occur in continuous neighborhoods not captured by fixed clusters, but testing must still respect sample replication and multiplicity.
coreConcept: Differential abundance methods test cell-state neighborhoods or populations across samples using sample-aware designs; results depend on representation and sampling.
minimalExample: Test whether graph neighborhoods have consistent count shifts across treated versus control patients.
commonWrongPractice: Treat neighborhood cell membership as independent or describe an abundance association as lineage expansion mechanism.
reviewerAttack: Assess sample balance, neighborhood overlap, FDR, annotation sensitivity, and whether shifts are driven by one sample.
whenToUse: State shifts that may cut across cluster boundaries.
whenNotToUse: Do not interpret capture-frequency differences as proliferation without orthogonal evidence.
transferPrompt: State whether your abundance target is a predefined population or a data-derived neighborhood.

title: Trajectory inference limits
whyItMatters: A static snapshot can support an ordering compatible with transition, but not observe lineage or causal progression directly.
coreConcept: Pseudotime and trajectory topology depend on sampled states, root choice, features, preprocessing, and method assumptions.
minimalExample: Cells ordered from progenitor-like to differentiated expression states suggest a continuum but do not prove individual cells traverse it.
commonWrongPractice: Call a UMAP path development, infer direction without information, or map between-patient differences onto within-cell dynamics.
reviewerAttack: Justify root/topology, show robustness across methods/features, and seek temporal, lineage, velocity, or perturbation support.
whenToUse: Hypothesis generation about continuous state structure and candidate progression.
whenNotToUse: Do not claim lineage fate or transition rates from cross-sectional pseudotime alone.
transferPrompt: Rewrite your trajectory conclusion using 'consistent with' and name the missing temporal evidence.

title: Cell-cell communication limitations
whyItMatters: Ligand–receptor co-expression generates hypotheses; it does not demonstrate secretion, binding, signaling, or functional effect.
coreConcept: Communication tools combine expression, curated interactions, and model assumptions; evidence is strongest when spatial, protein, perturbation, and phenotype data converge.
minimalExample: Tumor ligand and macrophage receptor expression suggests a candidate axis for perturbation.
commonWrongPractice: Call inferred edges active signaling and compare edge counts without accounting for cell abundance/expression detectability.
reviewerAttack: Validate protein/location, perturb ligand/receptor, show downstream response, and control for abundance and database choice.
whenToUse: Prioritize plausible intercellular hypotheses.
whenNotToUse: Do not use inference alone to establish mechanism or therapeutic efficacy.
transferPrompt: For one inferred axis, specify an orthogonal localization test and a functional perturbation.

title: Spatial colocalization ≠ mechanism
whyItMatters: Proximity supports opportunity for interaction, but shared niches and tissue architecture can generate colocalization without causal communication.
coreConcept: Separate descriptive adjacency, adjusted spatial association, molecular interaction, and functional mechanism as distinct evidence levels.
minimalExample: Exhausted T cells near macrophages may reflect both cells accumulating at invasive margins rather than macrophages causing exhaustion.
commonWrongPractice: Treat spot-level co-expression or nearest-neighbor enrichment as direct signaling.
reviewerAttack: Control tissue compartment/density, validate resolution, test molecular direction, and add perturbation or functional readout.
whenToUse: Map architecture and prioritize mechanistic hypotheses.
whenNotToUse: Do not claim causal interaction from colocalization alone.
transferPrompt: Place your spatial result on the evidence ladder from expression to functional perturbation.

title: Multi-omics integration
whyItMatters: Integration can reveal shared structure but can also align technical effects, erase modality-specific biology, or overstate cross-layer confirmation.
coreConcept: Define the integration estimand, sample matching, scaling, missing modalities, confounding, and independent validation before choosing an algorithm.
minimalExample: Matched tumor RNA and protein data test whether a subtype has concordant pathway-level shifts across layers.
commonWrongPractice: Concatenate features, cluster, and call modalities mutually validating because the same samples drove both results.
reviewerAttack: Show modality-specific QC/effects, sample alignment, robustness to method/weights, held-out validation, and discordant findings.
whenToUse: When cross-layer information addresses a scientific question better than separate analyses.
whenNotToUse: Do not integrate merely to increase technical complexity or when sample identities/design are incompatible.
transferPrompt: Write the specific claim that requires two modalities and what each contributes independently.

title: Discovery vs validation
whyItMatters: Evidence generated and judged in the same data is discovery, even when split into several analysis figures.
coreConcept: Validation evaluates a locked claim, marker, cutpoint, signature, or model in independent or properly resampled data with prespecified metrics.
minimalExample: Select a protein signature in cohort A, lock its formula, and evaluate it unchanged in cohort B.
commonWrongPractice: Retune features or thresholds in the validation set and report the tuned performance as validation.
reviewerAttack: What exactly was locked, when, and which data remained untouched until final evaluation?
whenToUse: Biomarkers, subtypes, models, signatures, and exploratory omics findings.
whenNotToUse: Technical replication or repeating a measurement in the same specimens is not external biological validation.
transferPrompt: Name one frozen object and one untouched dataset needed to validate your central claim.

title: Data leakage
whyItMatters: Information unavailable at prediction time or from evaluation data can enter model training and produce unrealistically high performance.
coreConcept: Define prediction time and split at the independent unit before any learned preprocessing, selection, imputation, augmentation, or tuning.
minimalExample: Normalize using all patients before cross-validation; validation patients influence the training transformation.
commonWrongPractice: Randomly split cells from the same patients across folds or use post-outcome variables as predictors.
reviewerAttack: Audit the pipeline chronologically and repeat every learned step inside training folds grouped by patient.
whenToUse: Any predictive, classification, or machine-learning workflow.
whenNotToUse: Not all use of global fixed constants is leakage; distinguish learned information from prespecified transformations.
transferPrompt: Write what information is available at the exact deployment prediction time.

title: Feature selection leakage
whyItMatters: Selecting features using all outcomes lets test-fold information shape the model before evaluation.
coreConcept: Supervised feature selection is part of model fitting and must occur independently within each training resample.
minimalExample: Run differential expression on all patients, retain 50 genes, then cross-validate a classifier: the CV estimate is contaminated.
commonWrongPractice: Describe feature selection as preprocessing and perform it once before resampling.
reviewerAttack: Provide pipeline code/order and show nested selection in each resample plus final locked feature set.
whenToUse: High-dimensional omics model development.
whenNotToUse: A genuinely external, prespecified feature set may be fixed outside resampling if its derivation did not use current outcomes.
transferPrompt: Move every outcome-aware feature step inside the training-fold boundary in your workflow diagram.

title: Cross-validation misuse
whyItMatters: Cross-validation estimates a full procedure only when splitting matches independence and all tuning is nested.
coreConcept: Use grouped splits for clustered samples, nested CV for hyperparameter/model selection, and report variability rather than the best fold.
minimalExample: All cells from a patient remain in one fold; inner folds tune the model, outer folds estimate performance.
commonWrongPractice: Tune and report performance on the same CV, split repeated measures across folds, or repeat until a favorable seed appears.
reviewerAttack: Specify split unit, stratification, nesting, repeats, metric aggregation, and handling of preprocessing.
whenToUse: Internal validation when independent external data are unavailable.
whenNotToUse: CV cannot demonstrate transportability to different centers or eras.
transferPrompt: Name the outer split unit and every operation inside the inner tuning loop.

title: Unsupervised clustering stability
whyItMatters: A visually clean cluster solution may change with preprocessing, features, resolution, or sample perturbation.
coreConcept: Assess whether the chosen structure is reproducible under resampling and reasonable analysis alternatives, and whether clusters exist across biological samples.
minimalExample: Bootstrap samples/features, compare co-clustering, and test whether a subtype appears across centers rather than one batch.
commonWrongPractice: Choose k by the most attractive heatmap, then test outcomes as if k were prespecified.
reviewerAttack: Show stability, sensitivity, batch/sample composition, external assignment, and uncertainty for borderline samples.
whenToUse: Molecular subtyping, cell states, and latent structure discovery.
whenNotToUse: Stability does not prove biological or clinical relevance; a stable technical artifact remains possible.
transferPrompt: Choose two perturbations that your claimed subtype should survive.

title: Multiple candidate model selection
whyItMatters: Trying many algorithms, endpoints, signatures, and thresholds makes the winning model's reported performance optimistic.
coreConcept: Treat the entire candidate-search process as one adaptive procedure and evaluate it with nested resampling or untouched data.
minimalExample: Twenty algorithms are tuned; inner CV chooses one and outer CV evaluates the choice process.
commonWrongPractice: Report only the best cross-validated model without accounting for the comparison that selected it.
reviewerAttack: List all candidates and tuning decisions, use nested evaluation, and compare with a simple clinical baseline.
whenToUse: Algorithm benchmarking and signature/model selection.
whenNotToUse: Do not add models without scientific or deployment rationale merely to search for a higher metric.
transferPrompt: Count every model family, feature set, endpoint, and cutpoint tried before choosing the reported result.

title: Causal language calibration
whyItMatters: Associational designs do not automatically support claims that an exposure changes an outcome.
coreConcept: Match verbs to design and evidence: associated/predictive, spatially compatible, perturbation effect, rescue, in vivo effect, and clinical effect are different levels.
minimalExample: Retrospective expression–survival association supports 'associated with prognosis,' not 'drives progression.'
commonWrongPractice: Use 'regulates,' 'promotes,' or 'mediates' after cross-sectional correlation and pathway enrichment.
reviewerAttack: Identify the intervention, counterfactual contrast, temporality, confounding control, and functional evidence.
whenToUse: Every abstract, discussion, figure title, and AI-generated narrative.
whenNotToUse: Avoid so much hedging that a randomized or well-controlled perturbation result loses its actual estimand.
transferPrompt: Underline causal verbs in one draft paragraph and align each with the strongest evidence level.

title: Events and information in survival models
whyItMatters: For time-to-event models, information is driven mainly by observed events, not total enrollment alone.
coreConcept: Model complexity, censoring, predictor distribution, effect size, and events determine precision; simple rules are diagnostic, not universal guarantees.
minimalExample: A cohort of 1,000 with 35 deaths may not support a 20-parameter prognostic model.
commonWrongPractice: Cite total n while omitting event counts and effective parameters.
reviewerAttack: Report events, candidate parameters, penalization, uncertainty, and resampling-based optimism.
whenToUse: Planning and auditing survival analyses and prediction models.
whenNotToUse: Do not apply a fixed events-per-variable cutoff as a substitute for design-specific power/simulation.
transferPrompt: Count outcomes and effective parameters—not just named variables—in your primary survival model.

title: Analytical vs clinical validation
whyItMatters: A clinically associated biomarker is not deployable if the assay is unreliable, and an accurate assay is not necessarily clinically useful.
coreConcept: Analytical validity concerns measurement performance; clinical validity concerns association/prediction; clinical utility concerns improved decisions or outcomes.
minimalExample: A protein signature requires reproducible assay measurements, external prognostic validation, then evidence that using it changes beneficial decisions.
commonWrongPractice: Use independent staining of the same specimens as proof of clinical validation or utility.
reviewerAttack: Separate measurement reproducibility, locked cutoff/model validation, and decision-impact evidence.
whenToUse: Biomarker and diagnostic/translational studies.
whenNotToUse: Do not demand clinical utility trials for early discovery claims; calibrate claim stage instead.
transferPrompt: Place your biomarker at analytical validity, clinical validity, or clinical utility, and name the next missing evidence.

title: Model updating after validation
whyItMatters: Transported models often need recalibration, but updating changes the object being evaluated.
coreConcept: Report untouched validation first; then update intercept/baseline hazard, slope, or coefficients with adequate local data and validate the updated model.
minimalExample: A model ranks well but overpredicts risk; adjust calibration-in-the-large and reassess on separate or resampled data.
commonWrongPractice: Tune on the external cohort and call the resulting metric external validation.
reviewerAttack: Distinguish original performance, updating method, effective sample size, and validation of the updated model.
whenToUse: Deployment in a population with calibration drift.
whenNotToUse: Updating cannot rescue predictors unavailable or defined differently at deployment without redesign.
transferPrompt: Specify what would remain locked and what may be updated for your target site.

title: Batch-correction sensitivity
whyItMatters: Integration settings can change neighborhoods, clusters, and differential findings.
coreConcept: Evaluate conclusions across plausible correction strategies and inspect both batch mixing and conservation of expected biology.
minimalExample: Repeat subtype analysis with uncorrected covariate-aware models and two integration choices.
commonWrongPractice: Pick the embedding with maximal mixing and proceed without quantitative or biological sensitivity checks.
reviewerAttack: Demonstrate conclusion stability and show that expected controls and rare states were not erased.
whenToUse: Integrated atlas and cross-cohort omics analyses.
whenNotToUse: Do not correct variables that are identical to the biological contrast of interest.
transferPrompt: Name one biological signal that correction should preserve and one technical pattern it should reduce.

title: Spatial resolution and deconvolution
whyItMatters: A spatial spot may contain several cell types; inferred cell-type signals inherit reference and mixture assumptions.
coreConcept: Match claims to platform resolution and validate deconvolution using histology, marker coherence, simulations, or orthogonal single-cell/imaging data.
minimalExample: A tumor–immune boundary spot contains both compartments; co-expression is not necessarily within one cell.
commonWrongPractice: Describe spot-level expression as single-cell expression or treat deconvolved proportions as observed counts.
reviewerAttack: Report resolution, reference compatibility, uncertainty, histologic validation, and sensitivity to deconvolution method.
whenToUse: Spot-based spatial transcriptomics and cell-type mapping.
whenNotToUse: Do not infer subcellular localization from multicellular spots.
transferPrompt: Write the smallest spatial unit actually observed by your platform and the finest claim it supports.

title: Reporting guideline vs study rigor
whyItMatters: Complete reporting makes a study auditable but does not by itself remove bias or validate the methods.
coreConcept: Use reporting checklists to expose design and analysis decisions, then judge validity with design-specific reasoning and risk-of-bias tools.
minimalExample: A fully STROBE-compliant retrospective study can still have unmeasured confounding.
commonWrongPractice: Claim methodological quality because a checklist score is high.
reviewerAttack: Separate reporting completeness from bias, precision, applicability, and causal identification.
whenToUse: Manuscript preparation and structured appraisal.
whenNotToUse: Do not convert guideline items into an unvalidated total quality score.
transferPrompt: Name one well-reported limitation in your study that reporting cannot repair.
